content: 1. A study involving 567 participants compared a 7-day placebo regimen with no measurement of compliance, quality of life, or HSV-2 severity/pain. The outcomes were not assessed in terms of these parameters. 2. The WHO guidelines (Recommendation 3 and 4) for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) were evaluated. The quality of evidence was moderate, with an estimated effect of 250 more cases per 1000 (ranging from 18 fewer to 128 more) based on confidence intervals (CI). 3. Many studies had unclear blinding or randomization methods, and some participants were lost to follow-up, which may have introduced bias. 4. One study with 329 participants reported similar rates of non-serious adverse events in both treatment and placebo groups, with no serious adverse events observed. 5. A systematic review by Le Cleach et al. (2014) assessed oral antiviral therapy for preventing genital herpes outbreaks in immunocompetent, non-pregnant patients. The review included multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs). 6. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by Aoki et al. (2006) evaluated single-day, patient-initiated famciclovir therapy for recurrent genital herpes. The study demonstrated efficacy and safety. 7. Baeten et al. (2012) conducted a trial on episodic acyclovir therapy for genital ulcers in HIV-1 seronegative, HSV-2 seropositive African women. The study showed clinical and virologic responses. 8. Fife et al. (2008) investigated valacyclovir for suppressing HSV-2 genital herpes in newly diagnosed patients. The international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study confirmed its effectiveness. 9. Goldberg et al. (1986) assessed oral acyclovir for episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes, demonstrating its efficacy and safety. 10. Leone et al. (2010) compared one-day famciclovir with placebo in Black patients with recurrent genital herpes. The study confirmed the efficacy of famciclovir. 11. Paz-Bailey et al. (2009) demonstrated that episodic acyclovir therapy improved healing and reduced HIV shedding in men as part of syndromic management. 12. Phiri et al. (2010) evaluated the impact of acyclovir on ulcer healing, genital and plasma HIV-1 RNA, and HSV-2 DNA in patients with genital ulcer disease in Malawi. The study showed significant benefits. 13. Bodsworth et al. (1997) compared valacyclovir (500 mg twice daily for 5 days) with acyclovir (200 mg five times daily for 5 days) for episodic treatment of genital herpes. Both regimens were effective. 14. Tyring et al. (1998) compared valacyclovir (1000 mg twice daily for 5 days) with acyclovir (200 mg five times daily for 5 days) in immunocompetent patients with recurrent genital herpes. The study confirmed the efficacy of both treatments. 15. Chosidow et al. (2001) compared acyclovir (200 mg five times daily for 5 days) with famciclovir (125 mg twice daily for 5 days) in immunocompetent patients. The study found comparable efficacy. 16. Leone et al. (2002) compared a 3-day valacyclovir regimen (500 mg twice daily) with a 5-day regimen (500 mg twice daily) for episodic treatment of genital herpes. Both regimens were effective. 17. Saia et al. (1999) assessed the equivalence of valacyclovir 1000 mg once daily versus 500 mg twice daily for episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes. The study confirmed similar efficacy. 18. Spruance et al. (1996) conducted a large-scale, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial of valacyclovir for episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes. The study demonstrated its effectiveness. 19. Sacks et al. (1996) evaluated patient-initiated, twice-daily oral famciclovir for early recurrent genital herpes. The randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial confirmed its efficacy. 20. Straus et al. (1986) compared weekend and daily regimens of oral acyclovir for suppressing recurrent genital herpes. Both regimens were effective. 21. The WHO guidelines (Recommendation 3 and 4) for episodic acyclovir therapy versus no treatment in people living with HIV showed moderate-quality evidence. The results were imprecise due to wide confidence intervals and few events across studies. 22. A pooled analysis by Weiss et al. (2011) of three RCTs in sub-Saharan Africa demonstrated the efficacy of episodic therapy for genital herpes in reducing symptoms and improving healing. 23. Abudalu et al. (2008) compared single-day famciclovir therapy with a 3-day valacyclovir regimen for recurrent genital herpes. The randomized, double-blind trial confirmed the efficacy of both treatments. 24. The quality of evidence for episodic valacyclovir versus episodic famciclovir was moderate, with both treatments showing similar efficacy in reducing the duration of viral shedding and symptoms. 25. Compliance with treatment regimens was generally high across studies, with most participants completing the prescribed courses. 26. Adverse events, including headache, nausea, and gastrointestinal symptoms, were reported at similar rates across treatment groups. Serious adverse events were rare. 27. The WHO guidelines recommend episodic antiviral therapy for managing genital herpes simplex virus infections, with valacyclovir, acyclovir, and famciclovir being effective options.
